title: Anaya Bangar Gets Cricket Australia Clearance, Eyes WBBL Spot From March 2027
excerpt: The daughter of former India batting coach Sanjay Bangar has been cleared to play community cricket in Australia immediately and could become eligible for elite women's cricket by March 2027.
body:
• Cricket Australia has confirmed Anaya Bangar's eligibility for elite women's cricket from March 2027 under its transgender inclusion policy
  • Bangar, 25, who played U-19 cricket for Mumbai before her transition, can compete in community cricket immediately
  • The BCCI has not responded to Bangar's request to play women's cricket in India, leaving Australia as her path forward

Anaya Bangar, the 25-year-old daughter of former India all-rounder and batting coach Sanjay Bangar, has received official clearance from Cricket Australia to resume competitive cricket — a ruling that opens a pathway to the Women's Big Bash League starting March 2027.

Bangar, who underwent gender-affirming surgery in March 2026 after beginning hormone replacement therapy in 2022, received the confirmation under Cricket Australia's Inclusion of Transgender and Gender Diverse Players in Elite Cricket Policy. An expert panel comprising CA's head of integrity Jacqui Partridge, anti-doping medical officer Dr. Peter Harcourt, and team doctor Dr. Pip Inge reviewed her case and medical records before granting clearance.

"I am now eligible to play in the Women's Big Bash League in Australia from March 2027 onwards. For me, this is incredibly emotional because there was a point when I genuinely believed I had lost cricket forever."

— Anaya Bangar, to Bombay Times

A Career Interrupted

Before her transition, Bangar played U-19 cricket for Mumbai — following in the footsteps of her father, who represented India in 12 Tests and 15 ODIs and served as the national team's batting coach from 2014 to 2019. Her connection to the sport runs deep, and the prospect of walking away permanently was, by her own account, the hardest part of her transition.

"Cricket has been such a fundamental part of my identity since childhood, and having to step away from the sport after my transition was one of the hardest things I experienced," she told Bombay Times. "This isn't simply about being included in a women's league. It represents the possibility of returning to the sport I deeply love."

The Road to the WBBL

Under Cricket Australia's policy, Bangar must maintain her serum testosterone concentration below 10 nmol/L continuously for at least 12 months to qualify for elite cricket. She will need to provide a blood test upon arrival in Australia confirming compliance. Until March 2027, she is eligible to play in Premier Cricket competitions in any Australian state or territory.

But eligibility alone does not guarantee a roster spot. The WBBL operates an overseas-player contracting and draft system similar to the IPL and WPL, where franchises select from a pool of available international players.

"I still have to train, compete, perform and earn that opportunity," Bangar told The Indian Express. "The next challenge is to get myself into the best possible physical and competitive shape and put myself in a position to be considered by a WBBL franchise."

BCCI Silence and the Indian Impasse

Bangar had first approached the Board of Control for Cricket in India to ask whether she could play women's cricket domestically. The BCCI has not responded with a clear policy. According to officials quoted by The Indian Express, the board is encountering this scenario for the first time and has yet to formally take a stand on allowing transgender women in domestic cricket.

The International Cricket Council barred individuals who underwent male puberty from elite women's international cricket in 2023 — a policy that effectively ended the international career of Canada's Australian-born opening batter Danielle McGahey after just six women's international games. McGahey had become the first transgender cricketer to play an officially sanctioned international match.

What This Means for Indian Cricket

Bangar's case puts pressure on the BCCI to develop a formal transgender inclusion framework for domestic competition. While Cricket Australia has laid out clear criteria — centered on testosterone levels and medical documentation — India's cricket governing body has no equivalent policy in place.

For now, Australia offers Bangar the clearest path back to competitive cricket. She has already begun preparing for community-level matches and plans to use the coming months to build her case for a WBBL franchise contract.

"It is a great day for me, especially after knowing the fact that I can play cricket," she told The Indian Express. "There was a stage when I thought I would never play cricket again, but thanks to Cricket Australia, it has given me another chance."
